gaps.sentence: The lecture was ___ attended than the organisers had hoped.
gaps.explanation: 'Well attended' compares with the adverb: less well attended.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the two proposals has been approved so far.
gaps.explanation: 'Neither of the two' — 'none' is for three or more.

gaps.sentence: ___ lakes in this region freeze in winter.
gaps.explanation: 'Most lakes' speaks about lakes in general; 'most of' would need 'the lakes'.

gaps.sentence: I'd love ___ help with the decorating, if you're free.
gaps.explanation: 'Some' is used in requests and hopes where the speaker wants agreement.

gaps.sentence: Only ___ people attended the talk, which was disappointing.
gaps.hint: countable plural; 'only a few' is the natural pattern
gaps.explanation: 'Only a few people' is the standard way to say a small number; 'only few' is not used.

gaps.sentence: She's very fussy — she refuses to eat ___ green.
gaps.hint: after 'refuse' the clause is negative in meaning
gaps.explanation: Verbs like refuse, deny and avoid create a negative context, so 'anything' is used.

gaps.sentence: Don't rush — we've got ___ of time.
gaps.hint: fixed pattern: ___ of time (no article needed)
gaps.explanation: 'Plenty of time' needs no article; 'lot of time' would need 'a', and 'much of time' needs 'the'.

gaps.sentence: ___ attempts were made to contact her.
gaps.explanation: 'Several' is used with countable plurals; 'much', 'little' and 'a great deal of' need uncountables.
